work.text: … the scroll in the Cleveland Museum [which] is dated 1662. The [composition] consists mainly of [epidendrum (orchids)] but includes also two slender branches of bamboo and a garden rock. It is exquisitely balanced in [design] as well as in tone and executed [with] the utmost [refinement].
work.lead: Sirén, among Shitao’s earliest dated paintings:

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V

work.text: Between are numerous orchids and one spray of bamboo. All are thrown on the paper in Shih-t’ao’s favorite “one stroke” style with no worries as to the finish or detail. Rather the life of the plants and so of nature itself is portrayed, fulfilling the artist’s written aims.

source.author: Sherman E. Lee
source.title: “Rocks, Orchids, and Bamboo” by Shih-t’ao
source.publisher: The Bulletin of the Cleveland Museum of Art 41, no. 1 (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: Shih-t’ao (also known as Tao-chih) is one of the four great individualists who glorify the seventeenth century, the others being Chu Ta, K’un-ts’an, and Kung Hsien. The former two were of the Ming royal blood and all chose the life of a recluse as a protest against the new … Manchu dynasty.

source.author: Sherman E. Lee
source.title: “Rocks, Orchids, and Bamboo” by Shih-t’ao
source.publisher: The Bulletin of the Cleveland Museum of Art 41, no. 1 (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: Near a cliff there are a few pieces of stone, A sweet smell floats from the orchid plants: Catching this mood in painting, There is a quiet feeling at my brushtip.
matters.lead: Shitao’s poem at the end of the scroll:

source.author: Shitao (Shih-t‘ao)
source.title: Inscription on Rocks, Orchids, and Bamboo, 1662
source.publisher: translated by Wen Fong in Sherman E. Lee, “‘Rocks, Orchids, and Bamboo’ by Shih-t’ao”, The Bulletin of the Cleveland Museum of Art 41, no. 1 (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: The far extending sinuous leaves of the magnificent plants, which are bending and [undulating] with the suppleness [of] living [nerves, seem] to reflect the sensitiveness and shifting thoughts of the painter like [the] strings of a violin vibrating under the touch of a master[’s] bow.

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V
